approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
approach_variants.notes: From the signed Blue Lake trailhead on the highway a short distance west of Washington Pass, follow the Blue Lake Trail about a mile and a half to a small meadow, then take the climbers' boot path that breaks off just past a small stream. That path climbs through slabs, talus and meadow toward the gully descending from between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. Where the path splits, bear left and continue up the gully to the notch at its top. The gully commonly holds snow and ice into late June and is a known rockfall channel, particularly during spring and early-summer snowmelt, so move through it efficiently and keep helmets on. The notch at the top of the gully is where the route starts. Access work on the lower path has reduced the time spent in the loose ground, but the gully itself is still the part of the day worth hurrying through.
approach_variants.season: July through September. The approach gully commonly holds snow into late June, and the face itself stays wet after rain and freezes early and late in the season.
hazards: rockfall in the approach gully, especially during spring and early-summer snowmelt
sustained, steeper climbing than the standard line with correspondingly less margin
a long, wandering second pitch prone to serious rope drag
a small, exposed summit shared with parties on the neighbouring routes
north-facing rock that stays wet after rain
approach_variants.baseFinding: The hueco wall is where the two routes part, and this one goes right. The base is the top of the notch between Concord Tower and Liberty Bell, reached by the gully — if you scrambled left out of the gully a couple of hundred feet below the notch onto a broad sloping bench, you are on Liberty Bell's west side and on a different mountain's route entirely. From the notch, the first pitch follows a crack system to a large ledge with some small trees growing on it; that ledge with trees is the confirmation you are on the North Face and not somewhere else on the tower. The second pitch is the one that matters here. Move right on easy ground, then straight up on rock that sounds hollow and flaky, to a section of ten to fifteen feet of unprotectable blank wall covered in huge huecos with excellent holds. At the top of that hueco wall is the decision: the standard line steps left, and this variation continues right, up steeper crack and corner terrain to a prominent vertical crack, then traverses back left across the face to a large boulder. If you stepped left above the huecos, you are on the standard route at an easier grade, not on this variation. Expect severe rope drag on that long right-then-left pitch; extend everything.

pitch_detail.notes: Shares the standard North Face's opening crack-to-ledge pitch off the notch, though parties typically belay a bit further right on the ledge to line up for the direct finish above.

The direct ('Directisimo') line: a sustained crack running hands to off-width to chimney size, steeper and more direct than the standard route's diagonal left turn, with one section that breaks briefly onto the face where the crack pinches down partway up.
From the top of the crack, easy low-fifth-class ground leads up and left to the summit, rejoining the standard North Face's finish; protection is sparse once you leave the crack.
pitch_detail.anchor: 2-bolt summit anchor (rap chains, shared w/ North Face)

days.note: Same approach to the col/notch as the standard North Face. Share its first pitch, then break right into a sustained 5.8 crack-to-chimney crux pitch, finishing with an easy low-fifth pitch to the summit.
days.title: Car-to-car: North Face Var. Right (Directissimo)
days.objective: Climb the Directissimo variant of the North Face

itinerary.totalNote: A standard single day (about 9 hrs car-to-car); a bit slower than the easier 5.7 North Face due to the sustained 5.8 offwidth/chimney crux.
